items.title: Lego’s BrickLink marketplace has been offline for a week following ‘unusual activity’
items.summary:
Bricklink, a popular online marketplace that Lego bought in 2019 where fans can buy and sell parts and sets, has been down for a week and the company doesn't know when it will return. The team who runs the site has been sharing updates over the past week including estimates of when it will be back up. It was last expected to return on November 11th, according to Jay's Brick Blog, but a statement Lego shared to the site yesterday says there's currently no estimate of when BrickLink will be back online.

items.title: I reviewed the Apple HomeView, ask me anything
items.summary:
Getting up close and personal with the Apple HomeView. | Photo: Hunter McRae for The Verge	

Hi! I'm Jen Tuohy, The Verge's senior smart home reviewer. I've tested every smart display Amazon and Google have ever made, and for the past week I've been testing Apple's first: The $299 HomeView.
I put the tabletop and wall-mounted versions through their paces, on my kitchen counter, bedside table, in my office, and on my coffee table. I also mounted one as a smart home control panel in my entryway. I cooked with it, ran my smart home from it, took calls on it, and tested its new Siri AI capabilities. 
I also let my family loose on it, and my tech-averse husband was a big fan. My teenage daughter, less so. (Ask me why).

items.title: I tried Google’s AI glasses and Meta’s finally got real competition
items.summary:
It's a weird time to launch a new pair of smart glasses.
These last few years, Meta has been the dominant player in pushing a fragile smart glasses resurgence. Unfortunately, its privacy reputation led to the "pervert glasses" moniker. Smart glasses have never been more unpopular.
But in the past week, I've been demoing some new smart glasses from Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster. Some are retro chic frames. Others have the same Y2K vibe as the Matrix films. All were made by Samsung and have Google's Gemini built in via Android XR, Google's platform for smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets.

items.title: Apple’s HomeView is my new favorite smart display — but not my daughter’s
items.summary:
Apple’s first smart display is finally here. And it’s good.﻿ | Photo: Hunter McRae for The Verge	

The HomeView nails everything I want from a smart display. It's superb at controlling my smart home; it's an excellent hands-free kitchen companion, a good speaker, and a gorgeous digital photo frame. It's also the first Apple smart speaker with Siri AI, which is an improvement, if still slow at times. But Apple has fallen into the trap that hampers other smart displays I've tested: not content with doing its core functions well, it tries to do more, and that's where the friction creeps in.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy, affair scandals
items.summary:
Jensen Huang at GTC Berlin last month. | Photo: Soeren Stache / picture alliance via Getty Images	

Nvidia's board announced that Jensen Huang - its longtime co-founder, president, and CEO - has resigned after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to Huang. Following a late Wednesday night meeting, the board accepted Huang's letter of resignation as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately, with current CFO Colette Kress appointed interim CEO. Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013, with previous stops at Cisco and Microsoft.

items.title: Ring confirms its camera drone won’t have manual controls after crashing on CBS News
items.summary:
When (or if) Ring's security camera drone flies into our homes in January, you won't get the option to pilot it yourself. The Ring Drone Cam relies entirely on an "AI Pilot" system to follow pre-programmed routes and navigate autonomously around obstacles, with no manual control option available - and an embarrassing demonstration with CBS News might reveal why.
The video, broadcast on CBS Mornings and published on Threads, shows Ring founder Jamie Siminoff allowing technology reporter Jo Ling Kent to manually fly an early version of the drone via a mobile app with integrated controls.

items.title: United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
items.summary:
United says it won't let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns.
The company says it hasn't yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers' information or make purchases they didn't intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers - like having them attest that their bags don't have explosives.
